newsitem.title: UK: Cortecs drug achieves goals, fails to excite.
newsitem.headline: Cortecs drug achieves goals, fails to excite.

text.p: Data from the Anglo-Australian group Cortecs International Plc on a key drug to combat bone-wasting disease osteoporosis matched up to expectations, analysts said on Tuesday, but failed to ignite the group's share price.
Cortecs said late-stage trials of an oral version of the injectable anti-bone-wasting drug Calcitonin showed a "statistically significant reduction" in the rate that bone deteriorated.

The trials, which will continue for another two years, also established the optimum dose for the drug and appeared to show that it worked as well as an existing nasal spray version developed by Swiss giant Novartis AG.
The company hopes that the data, based on three months of trials on 212 women aged between 55 and 77, will be sufficient for it to seek European regulatory approval.

It believes that by presenting itself as an alternative and more attractive version of an existing drug rather than as an entirely new product it will speed up the approval process. An independent assessor will decide if the data is strong enough in the next few weeks.
However despite the apparently good news, Cortecs shares failed to live up to the hopes of some analysts, who had predicted that the stock could burst through the 400 pence barrier on positive news.
Although shares raced ahead by up to 56 pence following the announcement, they had drifted back to stand just 22 pence higher at 265-1/2 in late afternoon trading in a generally soggy biotech sector.

Thomas Geimer, analyst at Henry Cooke Lumsden, said Cortecs had achieved its goal of trying to prove that it could equal the impact of the Novartis drug, Miacalcic. However, he said there may be "fatigue" among investors, as well as continuing wariness about Cortecs among institutions. Yamaichi International analyst Erling Refsum said there was no doubt that the drug worked, and said the share price had enjoyed a strong run in recent months ahead of the data.
The stock has risen 48 percent this year, although it is still well down from its April 1996 peak of 450 pence.
"I think it is the filing and a U.S. licensing deal that will kick things into place" said Refsum.
Cortecs, which already has three international marketing partners for the deal, indicated to analysts that it was beginning talks with further partners immediately on the strength of the trial data.
Osteoporosis, which causes bones to become brittle and break or fracture easily, affects at least 200 million people worldwide, Cortecs said. It is particularly acute among women.

Sales of Calcitonin already total around $800 million a year, and analysts expect the market to grow substantially, both because of the ageing population and the onset of a replacement for painful injections.
Geimer said however that Cortecs is "still a very expensive company, and still has a long way to go to market this product".
He added: "The price for me is still ahead of itself, but they have at least done what they set out to do."
